title: Paged vs Flash attention: benchmarking runbook and troubleshooting
body:
Purpose:
This runbook captures a pragmatic, repeatable approach to comparing FlashAttention, paged (paged-KV) attention, and fused-QKV attention kernels in our serving runtime. It focuses on measurable throughput/latency differences, root-cause signals (kernel breakdowns, memory traffic), and actionable remediation steps for regressions observed in production.

Scope and high-level hypotheses:
- FlashAttention should reduce global memory traffic and kernel time for attention-heavy decodes, improving tokens/sec at medium-to-long sequence lengths.
- Paged attention reduces memory pressure for very long context by swapping KV pages in/out; it may increase latency variance and memcpy activity compared to FlashAttention for short sequences.
- Fused QKV + fused projection kernels reduce kernel launch overhead and memory copies; combined with FlashAttention they may yield best steady-state throughput but may complicate fallback paths.

Hardware/software baseline to record for every experiment:
- GPU model and driver: e.g., A100-SXM4 80GB, NVIDIA driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.x
- OS and kernel: Ubuntu 22.04, 5.x
- PyTorch: 2.2.x (or exact build), cuDNN: present version
- Compiler/clang/cuda toolkit used to build custom kernels
- Build tags: torch+cuda, compiled flash_attention commit sha, our runtime commit sha
- Environment flags: TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA=0, OMP_NUM_THREADS, NVTX_ENABLED hinting

Experiment matrix (examples) - iterate across these axes:
- Models: small (350M), medium (1.3B), large (7B)
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8 (for generation throughput)
- Prompt/seq lengths: 64, 512, 2048, 8192 (if model supports it)
- Generation lengths: 32, 128 tokens
- Attention kernel variants: baseline (reference aten), flash_attention, paged_attention (page sizes 128/256/512), fused_qkv on/off
- Quantization: bf16 / fp16 / int8 (if supported)
- Warmup iterations: 20; measured iterations: 100 (or until 1k tokens emitted)

Instrumentation and commands (recommended):
1) High-level perf runs (tokens/sec, p50/p95 latencies):
python -u benchmarks/serve_attention_bench.py \
  --model llama-7b \
  --batch 1 \
  --input-len 512 \
  --gen-len 128 \
  --attention flash \
  --fused-qkv true \
  --warmup 20 \
  --iters 100 
  > /tmp/bench_flash.out 2>&1

2) nv-nsight system-wide capture (recommended for intermittent stalls):
nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys_flash --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --capture-range=cpu:start,end python benchmarks/serve_attention_bench.py --...

3) PyTorch profiler for kernel-level breakdown:
from torch.profiler import profile, record_function, ProfilerActivity
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], record_shapes=True, profile_memory=True) as prof:
    with record_function("infer_step"):
        model.generate(...)
# export trace to chrome and analyze kernel list
prof.export_chrome_trace("/tmp/trace_flash.json")

4) Raw kernel sampling (nsamples) using ncu (Nsight Compute):
ncu --target-processes all --set full --launch-skip 10 --launch-count 50 -o /tmp/ncu_flash python ...

Signals to collect (and what they mean):
- tokens/sec and p50/p95 latency: overall throughput and tail behavior
- per-kernel time breakdown: identifies the attention kernel(s) consuming most time (flash_attn_cuda vs aten_mm etc.)
- GPU memory copy time (cudaMemcpy, D2H/H2D): indicates paging or memcpy overhead for paged-KV
- SM utilization and achieved FLOPs: measure kernel efficiency; low utilization on big matmuls suggests memory-bound ops or low occupancy
- L2 and L1 hit rates, DRAM throughput: high DRAM indicates poor locality (paged swapping or repeated KV loads)
- Warp issue efficiency, stall reasons (ranked): highlights memory or execution stalls
- CUDA kernel launch counts: too many small kernels can add overhead; fused kernels should lower this count

Typical failure modes and diagnostic recipes:
1) Throughput regression when switching from reference to flash:
- Symptom: tokens/sec drops, per-kernel times show many tiny kernels instead of one fused op.
- Check: kernel list in Profiler; if flash_attn kernels are launching but very short, config might be selecting scalar path.
- Actions: verify sequence length matches expected tile sizes; retry with batch sizes changed; enable larger sequence lengths to amortize kernel launch overhead.

2) High memcpy activity with paged attention:
- Symptom: cudaMemcpy times dominate; p95 latency spikes.
- Check: page size vs sequence length, page eviction counts in our telemetry, host-device transfers in nsys.
- Actions: try increasing page size (256->512), or pin memory pools, tune prefetch threshold, or enable async prefetch threads. Consider moving to in-GPU persistent KV for medium context sizes.

3) Fallback to reference kernels unexpectedly:
- Symptom: profiler shows aten::matmul or aten::bmm instead of flash kernels.
- Check: model dtypes (fp16 vs bf16), shapes that trigger algorithm guardrails, or kernel compile mismatches.
- Actions: ensure kernels are compiled for the target compute capability, retry with identical CUDA/PyTorch build, add asserts/logs in kernel selector to capture reasons for fallback.

Result recording template (CSV example):
run_id,timestamp,gpu,driver,model,batch,seq,gen_len,attention_variant,fused_qkv,page_size,tokens_per_sec,p50_ms,p95_ms,memcpy_ms,flash_kernel_ms,other_kernel_ms,notes
run_20250214_01,2025-02-14T16:12:00Z,A100-80GB,535.54,llama-7b,1,512,128,flash,true,,512.4,18.5,34.9,2.1,12.3,3.8,"warmup 20, prof export"

Best practices and gotchas:
- Always run at least 3 independent runs and report median; transient system noise (IO, driver GC) is common on shared infra.
- Warmup matters: first few iterations include JIT and kernel caching; exclude them from final numbers.
- Set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING only for debugging; profiling with it toggled will misrepresent concurrency. Use it only to correlate host->device timing.
- For paged attention, watch for host CPU bottleneck in page management threads; CPU-side metrics (context switches, scheduler delays) matter.
- Pin buffers and use pooled allocators to reduce allocation overhead during repeated decodes.

Follow-ups and automation ideas:
- Add a CI job that runs a small, fast matrix of (flash, paged, fused) nightly and uploads CSVs to S3 + a Grafana dashboard showing regressions.
- Instrument kernel selector to emit a telemetry line with reason codes when a variant is not used (e.g., mismatch dtype / seq length).
- Implement a micro-benchmark harness that can be launched in Kubernetes on different instance types with identical seed inputs for apples-to-apples.

Open questions to answer in future runs:
- At what sequence length / batch crossover does FlashAttention strictly beat paged-KV for our real customer workloads? (we need workload traces)
- How does fused_qkv interact with quantization pipelines for int8/4-bit?
- Is there a non-linear latency tail introduced by page prefetch races under bursty request patterns?

References and useful links:
- FlashAttention repository (implementation notes) - https://github.com/flash-attention/flash-attention
- PyTorch profiler guide - https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/profiler.html
- Nsight docs - https://developer.nvidia.com/nsight-systems

Notes to the reader:
This is a working runbook; expect iterative updates as we gather more traces and automate capture. Use the linked INF and GH artifacts above for run-specific scripts and raw traces. If you run into a new anomaly, add a new CSV row to the results folder and drop a short summary in the Slack channel #eng-serving-runtime for visibility.
